evidence.document_name: pubmed_42897642_PMC13682045_Circadian clock and its potential as a therapy for ischemic.pdf
evidence.document_content: Circadian clock and its potential as a therapy for ischemic heart disease Yiran Wang1, He Wang1, Ning Liu1, Jiayi Zhang2 and Bin Liu1* Abstract According to an epidemiological survey, myocardial infarction, ischemia-reperfusion injury, and aortic rupture usually occur in the morning and summer and are characterized by more severe symptoms and poorer prognosis. The occurrence, development, treatment difficulties, and poor prognosis of ischemic heart disease are closely related to circadian rhythm disorders and the abnormal transcription of circadian clock genes. Normal circadian rhythms regulate neurohumoral regulation and energy metabolism, thereby playing a protective or modulatory role in ischemic heart disease (IHD). HIF1α links the IHD and circadian signaling pathways through the hypoxia response element (HRE) and Per-Arnt-Sim (PAS) domains in gene promoters and enhancers. ​Introduction The effects of circadian rhythms are profound at both cellular and animal levels. Studies have shown that in mammals, 80% of genes show periodic expression lev­ els in at least one tissue or organ. Furthermore, 82.2% of genes exhibit rhythmic transcription and are concur­ rently identified by the U.S. Food and Drug Administra­ tion (FDA) as druggable targets. Consequently, circadian rhythm management may have significant implications for human health [1]. In accordance with their adaptation to Earth's 24-h rotation cycle, human organs with auton­ omous circadian clocks are divided into two categories: central and peripheral circadian organs. Following exter­ nal environmental changes, primarily based on light and dark signals, to peripheral receptors (such as the retina), the clock's central gene sequence transcription-trans­ lation feedback loop (TTFL), located in the suprachias­ matic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus, undergoes continuous transcription, translation, modification, accumulation, and degradation of gene products over a 24-h period [2]. This causes circadian rhythm oscillations in the body. This rhythm information is gradually trans­ mitted to peripheral clock tissues and organs, regulat­ ing several important physiological processes, including hormone secretion, energy metabolism, inflammation, immune response, and aging [3-7]. Full list of author information is available at the end of the article As a peripheral rhythm-regulating organ, the cardio­ vascular system is influenced by neurohumoral factors, electrophysiological characteristics, and energy metab­ olism. These factors are subject to regulation by both rhythm control center, autonomous circadian rhythms and peripheral oscillation-affected factors, including environmental light, temperature, feeding, oxygen lev­ els, sensory stimulation, wakefulness/sleep (includ­ ing sleep deprivation, sleep restriction, and shift work), and exercise [8-12]. A substantial body of research has demonstrated the pivotal role of the biological clock in the pathogenesis of a wide range of diseases, including metabolic syndromes, neoplasms, neurological disor­ ders, respiratory illnesses, cardiovascular conditions, and immune-inflammatory responses [13-15]. Nevertheless, the precise means of attaining a 24-h circadian rhythm within an organism, optimizing the efficacy of treatment • The Author(s) 2026. chunks.document_content: P Disease duration P β (95% CI) -CML/esRAGE 0.700(0.020,1.381) 0.044 - -0.004(-0.008,-0.001) 0.027 - (P < 0.05). AGEs are formed via non-enzymatic glyca­ tion (Maillard reaction) between reducing sugars and proteins, CML being the most abundant and well-char­ acterized species [22]. The observed higher serum CML in the T1D group is consistent with the effects of chronic hyperglycemia and the metabolic memory phenomenon, whereby AGEs may continue to accumulate even after glycemic control is achieved [23]. Methylglyoxal (MG) is a highly reactive dicarbonyl metabolite of glycolysis that reacts with protein arginine residues to form MG-H1 [24]. In our study, MG-H1 lev­ els did not differ significantly between groups, which is inconsistent with some previous reports. Kilhovd et al. reported increased serum MG-H1 in patients with type 2 diabetes [25], and Karachalias et al. demonstrated increased MG-H1 adducts in the retina of streptozoto­ cin-induced diabetic rats [24]. In the present study, the mean MG-H1 level in the diabetic group was numerically higher than that in the control group, though the differ­ ence was not statistically significant, which may be attrib­ uted to the limited sample size of this pilot study. conditions. Reduced e(lat) may suggest impaired relax­ ation in diabetic patients. No significant change was observed in e(sep), which may be explained by differ­ ences in myocardial fiber architecture: longitudinal and circular fibers abundant in the lateral wall are sparsely distributed in the interventricular septum [31].
